issues.legal_issue: A will is not established as valid merely by proving its execution when suspicious circumstances surrounding its making remain unexplained.
material_facts: The testator was ill and died the day after the will was made; he had lived with the beneficiaries for the preceding six months.

The will gave all of the testator’s property to the sons of one daughter and excluded his other daughter, although no sour or estranged relationship between that daughter and the testator was found and no reason for excluding her was recorded.
The beneficiary’s father took an active part in arranging the will and fetched the professional scribe.
Although the testator could sign, he placed a thumb impression on the will. The scribe testified that he did not speak with the testator or ask about his health when he arrived.

The will’s recital listed various assets, including a house, factory, machinery and bank deposits, although there was no evidence that the testator owned a house other than one already sold, or owned a factory, machinery or bank deposits.
The lower courts treated proof of execution and the testator’s thumb impression as sufficient to establish the will’s genuineness.
issues.conclusion: The suspicious circumstances were not dispelled, so the will was not established as authentic and valid. The appeal was allowed, the judgments below were set aside, and the suit seeking a declaration that the will was invalid was decreed.
issues.legal_principle: A person may freely bequeath property, but the propounder must establish that the testator had a disposing mind and knew and understood the property and beneficiaries involved. The absence of a reason for excluding a person with a similar claim may cast suspicion on the disposition, and a propounder’s active participation raises a further strong suspicion. Proof of execution, including evidence from a scribe or attesting witness or proof of a thumb impression, does not by itself establish validity where suspicious circumstances remain; the court must be satisfied both as to execution and authenticity. The Court relied on H. Venkatachalliah v. N. Themmajamma, AIR 1959 SC 443, and Kalyan Singh v. Smt. Chhoti, [1989] JT 439. The judgment identifies the Indian Succession Act, 1925, but cites no specific provision.

rule.if: testamentary_will_dispute and testator_knew_property_and_beneficiaries and suspicious_circumstances and propounder_active_involvement and suspicious_circumstances_unresolved

predicates.testamentary_will_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a testamentary will is valid.
predicates.testator_knew_property_and_beneficiaries: The evidence concerns whether the testator knew and understood the property being disposed of and the people who would benefit.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances: Circumstances surrounding the will, such as illness near death, unexplained exclusion of a similarly entitled person, or an implausible recital of assets, cast doubt on whether the disposition was voluntary and authentic.
predicates.propounder_active_involvement: The person seeking to establish the will took an active part in arranging or making it.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_unresolved: The person seeking to establish the will did not adequately explain or dispel the circumstances casting doubt on it.

issues.definition: When a will is disputed, the testator’s understanding must be assessed and, if suspicious circumstances and active involvement by the propounder are present and remain unexplained, the will is not established as valid.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere with a lower court’s finding of fact when it results from an erroneous application of law and is apt to cause a miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The appeal was brought by special leave against the lower courts’ findings that the will was genuine.

The lower courts treated proof of execution as sufficient and did not properly assess the suspicious circumstances or the applicable standard of scrutiny where a daughter was disinherited in favour of grandchildren through another daughter.
The Supreme Court concluded that the lower courts had misapplied the legal principles governing proof of a will and that their approach could result in a miscarriage of justice.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court was justified in interfering under Article 136, set aside the judgments below, and allowed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Although the Court does not normally interfere with findings of fact, it may do so under Article 136 when a finding rests on an erroneous application of legal principle and is apt to result in a miscarriage of justice. Malkani v. Jamadar, AIR 1987 SC 767, was distinguished because the circumstances and the relationship between the competing beneficiaries differed.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and lower_court_fact_finding and erroneous_application_of_law and likely_miscarriage_of_justice

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal before the Supreme Court by special leave.
predicates.lower_court_fact_finding: The lower courts made a finding of fact that is challenged on appeal.
predicates.erroneous_application_of_law: The challenged finding was reached by applying a legal principle incorrectly.
predicates.likely_miscarriage_of_justice: The erroneous application of law is apt to cause a miscarriage of justice.

issues.definition: In an appeal by special leave, the Supreme Court may interfere with a lower court’s factual finding when that finding resulted from an erroneous application of law likely to cause a miscarriage of justice.
